text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Monday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-Nordic European Airlines will cancel its Stockholm-Brussels service from December 2 citing lack of demand by Swedish civil servants. Nordic entered into agreement with the Swedish government in July to fly 550 people per week between the two capitals and so save the government 40 million crowns, but civil servants preferred more expensive flights including those by Scandinavian Airlines System.

-The number of individuals investing in shares in Sweden has fallen by 100,000 since last year to four million, according to the Share Promotion association. It blamed higher tax rates on capital gains and funds this year for the reduction.

-Swedish businessman Adolf H Lundin, main shareholder in oil companies Sands Petroleum and IPC, is expanding his activities in the South China Sea between Malaysia and Vietnam. Lundin says he also has ambitious drilling programmes in Libya, Tanzania, Sudan and shortly in the Falkland Islands.

-Swedish Railways, SJ, will hold a management meeting today in an atmosphere of crisis caused by an annual loss of between 500 and 600 million crowns, with talk of cutbacks and up to 1,500 redundancies.

-Oxigene, a pharmaceuticval company which produces the cancer treatment Sensamide, will be introduced on the O-list of the Stockholm Bourse today. Interest in the share is strong, with a new issue oversubscribed five times. The 1.15 million shares to be listed are priced at 166.50 crowns.

-Swedbank has emerged as early leader among brokers bidding for the management of pension funds of local authorities in Sweden. This market is already worth 3.5 billion crowns, and Swedbank has won bids to manage 483 million crowns of funds to date.

-The board of Investor AB meets today to decide whether to seek a listing in New York, influenced perhaps by the relative lack of interest there in Astra AB and Scania AB shares. For instance when Scania in Sweden announced nine-month results recently sparking volume of 3.9 million shares, the busiest activity in its shares in Sweden, only 6,100 of them were traded in New York.

-Rights to live transmission of overseas soccer games are soaring beyond the financial means of some television companies and may in future be held only by pay-on-demand channels. Bourse-listed TV4 pays up to 5 million crowns a year for English Premiership games, and the rights to Italian Serie A games are believed to cost between 15 and 20 million crowns.
